nodes.ask: Red or painful eye, or sudden vision loss, at triage. First move?
options: ABCs and the story first: irrigate a splash at once, otherwise check vision
Visual acuity in both eyes first, then irrigate if the history turns up a splash
Measure the pressure in both eyes before anything else, to catch angle closure early
Dilate both pupils first so the whole retina can be seen, then take the history
nodes.chainStep: Airway, breathing and circulation first; ask about a chemical splash or an injury; irrigate a splash at once; everyone else has the vision checked in each eye, as acuity with glasses or a pinhole when the patient can read a chart
nodes.why: An injured patient is assessed airway, breathing and circulation first. A chemical splash is irrigated before anything else: irrigation takes priority over every diagnostic step, and the examination waits until the pH is neutral. Everyone else has the vision assessed in each eye, with glasses or a pinhole, because acuity sorts the routes. Measuring acuity before irrigating a splash spends the minutes that decide a burn, tonometry is one of the maneuvers to avoid in a possible open globe, and dilating first skips the history and acuity that choose the route.
nodes.note: Not in this version: closed-globe blunt injury (hyphema is only routed to ophthalmology), thermal and ultraviolet burns, lid lacerations, zoster ophthalmicus, optic neuritis, and transient monocular loss that has fully resolved.

outcomes.if: Unstable or major trauma; airway, breathing, circulation or consciousness at risk
Chemical splash; acid, alkali or another chemical in the eye
Possible open globe; a full-thickness wound, a peaked pupil, extruded tissue, or metal hammered on metal
Tense, bulging eye after trauma; vision falling, an afferent pupil defect, rock-hard lids
Lid cellulitis; swollen, red, warm lids, no globe injury, past the newborn period
Newborn with eye discharge; first 4 weeks of life
Everything else; no chemical, no open globe, no lid cellulitis

nodes.summary: Major trauma or an unstable patient: the primary survey and resuscitation come first, in the major trauma pathway (pw_trauma). Once it is safe, an injured eye gets a rigid shield with no pressure on the globe, acuity when it can be measured, and ophthalmology.

nodes.ask: Chemical splash in the eye. First move?
options: Irrigate now, after an anesthetic drop, until the pH reads 7.0 to 7.4
Visual acuity and a full slit lamp exam first, then start irrigating
Identify the exact chemical from the bottle first, then choose the irrigating fluid
Stain with fluorescein and grade the burn first, so the irrigation can be planned
nodes.chainStep: Topical anesthetic, then irrigate at once with lactated Ringer or saline for at least 30 minutes until the ocular surface pH is 7.0 to 7.4 on litmus; evert both lids and sweep the fornices; recheck the pH
nodes.why: Irrigation comes before every diagnostic step, and its timing matters more than the fluid: tap water is acceptable before arrival, and lactated Ringer, saline or a balanced salt solution in the department. Continue until the surface pH is neutral, 7.0 to 7.4 on litmus paper, for at least 30 minutes: a mild injury may need about 2 L, a severe one up to 10 L over 2 to 4 hours, and alkali usually more than acid. Evert the lids, double-evert the upper lid and sweep the fornices for particles, then recheck the pH. Acuity, the slit lamp, staining and grading wait for a neutral pH, and identifying the chemical never delays the rinse.

orders.dose: Lactated Ringer, 0.9% saline or a balanced salt solution; tap water before arrival rather than any delay
At least 30 minutes; about 2 L for a mild injury, up to 10 L over 2 to 4 hours for a severe one
Ocular surface pH 7.0 to 7.4 on litmus paper; recheck after irrigation
Evert both lids, double-evert the upper lid, sweep the fornices and remove every particle

nodes.summary: Chemical injury: irrigate first, until the pH is 7.0 to 7.4, then examine: acuity, the slit lamp with fluorescein, the eye pressure, and conjunctival blanching, which marks limbal ischemia. Systemic analgesia and immediate ophthalmology follow; the eye team starts lubricants, a topical antibiotic, a cycloplegic and a steroid, with amniotic membrane for moderate to severe burns.

options: Rigid shield, no pressure, antiemetic, IV antibiotics, nil by mouth, CT orbits, ophthalmology
Measure the eye pressure with a tonometer first to confirm the rupture before imaging
Pressure patch with antibiotic ointment, analgesia, and a CT of the orbits in the morning
MRI of the orbits to look for a hidden metal fragment, then call ophthalmology with the result
nodes.chainStep: Rigid shield over the eye, no pressure on the globe, no tonometry; antiemetic, analgesia, head of the bed at 30 degrees, nothing by mouth; systemic antibiotic prophylaxis; tetanus booster if needed; CT orbits; ophthalmology now for repair within 24 hours
nodes.why: Protect the eye and keep its pressure down: a rigid (Fox) shield, no pressure on the globe, and no tonometry, lid retraction or ultrasound, which can push the contents out. Antiemetics, analgesia and the head of the bed at 30 degrees prevent straining, food and fluids are withheld for surgery, and an open globe is a tetanus-prone wound. CT is the preferred imaging for a foreign body but never replaces the ophthalmic exam, and MRI is contraindicated while a metal fragment is possible. A protruding object stays until surgery, and repair should happen within 24 hours if at all possible.

nodes.summary: Open globe: a rigid shield, no pressure on the globe and no tonometry, antiemetic and analgesia, nothing by mouth, systemic antibiotics, tetanus cover, CT for a foreign body (never MRI while metal is possible), and ophthalmology for repair within 24 hours. A protruding object is left for the operating room.

nodes.ask: Tense, bulging eye after trauma, vision falling. Next?
options: Lateral canthotomy and cantholysis now, before any imaging
CT of the orbits first to confirm the hematoma, then decide
IV mannitol and acetazolamide, then recheck the vision in an hour
Pressure dressing over the eye and admission for observation
nodes.chainStep: Lateral canthotomy and cantholysis at the bedside now, under local anesthetic, ideally within 2 hours, without waiting for CT; antiemetic and analgesia; emergency ophthalmology; image afterwards if the eye does not clearly improve
nodes.why: Orbital compartment syndrome is a clinical diagnosis: a tense, proptosed eye after trauma with falling vision, an afferent defect or an eye pressure of 40 or more. When the optic nerve is threatened, imaging waits for decompression, and visual outcomes are better when it comes within the first 2 hours. Lateral canthotomy with cantholysis is the first-line bedside procedure. Mannitol, acetazolamide and steroids are adjuncts whose effect in this syndrome is not established, and observing the patient delays the decompression.

nodes.summary: Orbital compartment syndrome: lateral canthotomy and cantholysis at once, ideally within 2 hours, without waiting for imaging; antiemetic and analgesia; emergency ophthalmology. If the signs do not clearly improve, the orbit is imaged to find the hematoma and decompressed further surgically.

nodes.ask: Lid cellulitis, no globe injury. Next?
options: Eye movements and pain on moving them, proptosis, acuity, color vision and pupils
Oral antibiotics and home; the eye itself can be examined once the swelling settles
Contrast CT of the orbits first, and the eye exam once the scan is reported
Swab the lid and start antibiotic eye drops, then reassess tomorrow
nodes.chainStep: Vital signs; eye movements and pain on movement, proptosis, chemosis, acuity, color vision and pupils, to separate preseptal from orbital cellulitis
nodes.why: Lid swelling and redness occur in both, so they do not separate them. Pain with eye movement, restricted movement, double vision, proptosis, chemosis, falling acuity, poor color vision or an afferent pupil defect put the infection behind the septum. Sending the patient home before that exam can miss orbital cellulitis, the exam rather than a scan decides who needs imaging, and inadequate or delayed treatment can cost the eye or spread inside the skull.

outcomes.if: Lids only; eye moves fully without pain, vision and pupils normal

orders.dose: Age 1 year or more with mild disease: amoxicillin-clavulanate, cefpodoxime or cefdinir, with clindamycin or TMP-SMX where MRSA is a concern; usually 5 to 7 days; doses not stated in the sources read
Not stated in the sources read
Severe disease or under 1 year of age; also if outpatient treatment fails to improve within 24 to 48 hours, with a CT

outcomes.if: Orbital signs; pain on eye movement, restricted movement, proptosis or vision loss
Cannot be examined; lids swollen shut, or a child who will not cooperate

orders.dose: When preseptal and orbital cellulitis cannot be told apart, treat it as orbital cellulitis

nodes.summary: Preseptal cellulitis: oral antibiotics for 5 to 7 days in a well patient aged 1 year or more (amoxicillin-clavulanate, cefpodoxime or cefdinir, with clindamycin or TMP-SMX where MRSA is a concern), and a recheck. Admit for IV antibiotics and a CT if it is not better in 24 to 48 hours, if the child is under 1 year, or if orbital signs appear; when in doubt, treat as orbital cellulitis.

nodes.ask: Orbital signs, or no way to exclude them. Next?
options: Admit, IV vancomycin plus ceftriaxone, contrast CT orbits and sinuses, ophthalmology and ENT
Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate at home, with a review of the eye in 48 hours
Lumbar puncture first, then antibiotics once the CSF result is back

nodes.chainStep: Admit; IV vancomycin plus ceftriaxone, adding metronidazole when anaerobes are likely; contrast CT of the orbits and sinuses; ophthalmology and ENT; serial vision, pupils, color vision and motility
nodes.why: Orbital cellulitis needs admission, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, close checks of vision, pupils, color vision and motility, and early ophthalmology and ENT. A common empiric regimen is vancomycin for MRSA plus a broad beta-lactam such as ceftriaxone, with metronidazole for a dental source, chronic sinusitis, intracranial spread or an abscess. Contrast-enhanced CT of the orbits and sinuses is the usual first imaging: it shows the sinus disease and finds a subperiosteal or orbital abscess that may need drainage. Oral treatment at home is for preseptal disease, and antibiotics are not held back for other tests.

Worsening vision or an afferent defect, a large or non-medial subperiosteal abscess, an orbital abscess, intracranial spread, or no improvement after 24 to 48 hours of IV antibiotics goes to surgery; oral step-down after about 3 to 5 days, 2 to 3 weeks in all.

nodes.chainStep: Gram stain and culture of the discharge and a chlamydia test from the everted lid; gram-negative intracellular diplococci: ceftriaxone 25 to 50 mg/kg IV or IM once (max 250 mg) and a search for sepsis, arthritis and meningitis
nodes.why: Gram-negative intracellular diplococci on the smear justify treating for gonorrhea at once, after cultures, and the chlamydia test is taken from the everted lid at the same time. Gonococcal ophthalmia can perforate the globe, so one dose of systemic ceftriaxone is given and the baby is examined for disseminated infection, with infectious diseases input. Topical treatment alone is inadequate for either organism. A reaction to birth prophylaxis is mild and mucoid and settles within 48 hours, unlike a copious purulent discharge.

nodes.summary: Gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum (diplococci, usually days 2 to 5): ceftriaxone 25 to 50 mg/kg IV or IM once (max 250 mg), a search for disseminated infection, and infectious diseases input. Topical treatment alone is not enough; the mother and her partners are treated.

Chlamydial ophthalmia neonatorum: oral erythromycin base or ethylsuccinate 50 mg/kg/day in 4 doses for 14 days, a watch for pyloric stenosis, follow-up because a second course may be needed, and treatment of the mother and her partners; topical treatment alone is not enough.

nodes.chainStep: Pupils, intraocular pressure, slit lamp with fluorescein; ask about contact lenses, recent eye surgery, discharge and itch; a phenylephrine drop for sectoral redness once the pressure is known to be normal
nodes.why: Pain and photophobia, the pressure, the slit lamp with fluorescein, the response to phenylephrine and the acuity are the findings that separate a benign red eye from a dangerous one. Contact lens wear raises the risk of keratitis, and recent eye surgery points to endophthalmitis. Phenylephrine goes in only once the pressure is known to be normal. A steroid drop before the exam can worsen herpes keratitis and mask an infection, and fluorescein alone misses the pressure and the anterior chamber.

nodes.why: Acute angle closure is an emergency. Lower the pressure with aqueous suppressants first: topical timolol, an alpha-2 agonist and acetazolamide, IV when the patient is vomiting or speed matters. Pilocarpine works only once the pressure has come down and the iris is no longer ischemic, so it follows rather than leads, at 1 to 2%; intensive or stronger pilocarpine is avoided. Mannitol is the next step if the response is inadequate. Laser peripheral iridotomy is definitive, in the fellow eye too. Phenylephrine can worsen the attack, and a clinic appointment leaves an emergency untreated.

nodes.summary: Acute angle closure: timolol, an alpha-2 agonist and acetazolamide now, pilocarpine once the pressure falls, mannitol if it does not, an intensive topical steroid, and laser iridotomy in both eyes as soon as the cornea clears. If the pressure stays high the eye team breaks the attack with laser iridoplasty, paracentesis or lens extraction. A medication trigger is looked for.

options: Lenses out, no patch; topical fluoroquinolone now; ophthalmology within 24 hours

Topical prednisolone first to calm the inflammation, then antibiotics if it spreads

nodes.chainStep: Remove contact lenses; no patch; topical fluoroquinolone (ciprofloxacin 0.3%: 2 drops every 15 minutes for 6 hours, then every 30 minutes for the rest of day 1); ophthalmology within 24 hours, the same day if the ulcer is large, deep or central, for scrapings and fortified drops
nodes.why: Contact lens keratitis is most often Pseudomonas, which ciprofloxacin covers almost fully. A topical fluoroquinolone is used alone for small peripheral ulcers; large, deep or central ones get two antibiotics, usually fortified, after ophthalmology takes scrapings. Ophthalmology sees the patient within 24 hours, sooner when severe. Patching is not recommended, least of all when a contact lens caused the injury. A steroid is contraindicated in an untreated purulent infection, and systemic antibiotics have only a limited role in keratitis.

Antibiotics treat nothing here, and lubricants with an oral NSAID are the treatment for episcleritis, not iritis.

nodes.why: Evert the lids to find a retained foreign body. A topical antibiotic is the mainstay: an ointment such as erythromycin when no lenses are worn, a fluoroquinolone for Pseudomonas when they are. Patching is no longer recommended for most patients, least of all after a lens injury. Topical anesthetics are for the exam: they are toxic to the epithelium and not meant for self-administration. A steroid drop raises the risk of secondary infection. Pain that is not better in 24 hours needs ophthalmology urgently.

nodes.summary: Corneal abrasion: lid eversion, a topical antibiotic (erythromycin ointment, or a fluoroquinolone for a lens wearer), oral analgesia with or without a topical NSAID, no patch and no anesthetic drops to take home. Lens wearers see ophthalmology within 24 to 48 hours, and pain that is not better in 24 hours is seen urgently.

Episcleritis: redness that blanches with phenylephrine and a mild ache; most resolve on their own in 2 to 21 days. Artificial tears, an oral NSAID if needed, primary care follow-up for an underlying cause, and a return if the pain worsens, which suggests scleritis.

Scleritis: severe boring pain and redness that does not blanch. Emergency ophthalmology to start treatment and prevent scleral melting, a shield if the sclera is thin, and a search for systemic disease, present in about half: rheumatoid arthritis or granulomatosis with polyangiitis, for example.

Subconjunctival hemorrhage: reassurance and lubrication as needed; it usually clears in 1 to 2 weeks. Check the blood pressure, consider an INR on warfarin, and think of globe rupture after trauma or with a 360-degree bullous hemorrhage.

Viral conjunctivitis: supportive care with cold compresses and preservative-free artificial tears up to 8 times a day; no antibiotic. It is contagious for 1 to 2 weeks, so contact precautions. Pain or photophobia should raise the question of keratitis or uveitis.
Allergic conjunctivitis: a topical antihistamine, allergen avoidance, cold compresses and artificial tears; a mast cell inhibitor or an oral antihistamine for more severe symptoms.

Bacterial conjunctivitis: usually self-limited; a topical antibiotic such as polymyxin B with trimethoprim shortens it. Contact lens wearers get broad-spectrum cover such as a fluoroquinolone and close follow-up, because their conjunctivitis may be an early keratitis.

A dendrite, a hyphema or an embedded foreign body is not worked up in this pathway. Herpes simplex keratitis (a branching dendrite with end bulbs) gets an antiviral, no steroid drop, and ophthalmology within 24 hours; a hyphema goes to ophthalmology at once; a corneal foreign body is removed, or referred within 24 hours if removal fails.

nodes.ask: Hyperacute purulent conjunctivitis in an adult. Next?

Oral azithromycin 1 g alone, with lubricating drops for comfort

nodes.why: Hyperacute gonococcal conjunctivitis can involve the cornea and perforate it, so it is treated systemically at once: ceftriaxone 1 g IM as a single dose, the recommended regimen for gonococcal conjunctivitis, with a one-time saline lavage and infectious diseases input considered. Gonorrhea and chlamydia are treated together, so doxycycline is added unless chlamydia has been excluded. Topical treatment alone does not cover it, and a severe purulent discharge warrants prompt ophthalmology.

nodes.chainStep: Afferent pupil check, dilated fundus exam, visual fields, and bedside ocular ultrasound when there is no view; ask about flashes, floaters, a curtain, jaw claudication and scalp tenderness
nodes.why: The fundus decides the route: a pale retina with a cherry-red spot, a detached retina, blood and thunder, a swollen disc, or no view at all. Bedside ultrasound picks up a detachment with high sensitivity when blood hides the retina, and a vitreous hemorrhage alone does not cause an afferent defect. Sudden vision loss needs same-day assessment: a white eye does not make it benign, and a carotid study before the eye exam delays the diagnosis.

nodes.why: A central retinal artery occlusion is the eye's equivalent of an ischemic stroke, with a high early risk of a cerebral stroke, so it gets a stroke workup: brain imaging (about 30% show cerebral ischemia on MRI), carotid and cardiac sources, and vascular risk factors. ESR and CRP come first, to catch giant cell arteritis, which needs high-dose steroids at once. Ocular massage, paracentesis and pressure-lowering drops have not changed outcomes. Without an indication for anticoagulation, the prevention afterwards is antiplatelet.

nodes.summary: Non-arteritic central retinal artery occlusion, a stroke of the eye: a stroke-team workup (brain MRI, carotid duplex, echocardiogram, rhythm monitoring, vascular risk factors) and secondary prevention as for a TIA or minor stroke. Without an indication for anticoagulation or carotid surgery, that means 21 days of dual antiplatelet therapy, then a single agent; a symptomatic carotid stenosis on duplex goes to the stroke team for surgery. The stroke pathway (pw_stroke) carries the antiplatelet doses. Iris new vessels can follow within 1 to 2 months, so ophthalmology follows the eye.

Prednisone 10 mg daily, increased if the biopsy proves arteritis
Aspirin alone, and a rheumatology clinic appointment next month to discuss steroids

nodes.why: With threatened or lost vision, the ACR conditionally prefers pulse IV glucocorticoids over high-dose oral ones, and EULAR says pulsed methylprednisolone could be considered and starts treatment without waiting for confirmation when suspicion is strong. The biopsy can still show arteritis after steroids start, ideally within 2 weeks. Low-dose prednisone is not induction therapy, and delaying steroids risks the other eye.

nodes.summary: Giant cell arteritis with vision loss: glucocorticoids at once, pulse IV methylprednisolone then high-dose prednisone, without waiting for the biopsy. Confirmation, the taper and steroid-sparing treatment continue in the headache pathway's GCA route (pw_headache).

Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment (new floaters and flashes, then a spreading field loss): an ocular emergency. Same-day referral to a retina surgeon; whether the macula is still attached is one of the main factors in the visual outcome.

Posterior vitreous detachment with the retina attached: usually benign, but 8 to 22% have a retinal tear at the first exam, so ophthalmology does a prompt dilated peripheral exam and rechecks at 2 to 6 weeks. The patient returns at once for new floaters or flashes, a shadow or falling vision; an untreated symptomatic tear often goes on to detach.

Vitreous hemorrhage with the retina attached on ultrasound: prompt ophthalmology to find the cause (proliferative diabetic retinopathy, a posterior vitreous detachment with or without a tear, or trauma), but not an immediate emergency. The head of the bed is kept raised so the blood settles. A detachment on ultrasound changes the route to the retina surgeon.

Central retinal vein occlusion: referral to ophthalmology, preferably a retina specialist, and a workup for its causes (blood pressure, ESR, blood count, glucose, cholesterol, protein electrophoresis, renal and thyroid tests, ECG). No medical treatment is fully effective; anti-VEGF injections treat macular edema, and the ischemic form is checked monthly for 6 months for neovascular glaucoma.

outcomes.if: ESR and CRP raised, GCA symptoms; jaw claudication, scalp tenderness
ESR and CRP normal, no GCA symptoms; vascular risk factors

nodes.summary: Swollen optic disc with ESR and CRP normal and no GCA symptoms: likely non-arteritic ischemic optic neuropathy, whose workup is not in this pathway; ophthalmology.

A normal fundus and ultrasound with real, persisting vision loss points behind the eye, to the optic nerve or the brain; that workup is not in this pathway. A field loss in both eyes, such as a hemianopia, puts a stroke on the differential: the stroke pathway (pw_stroke).

cases.label: Vitreous hemorrhage
cases.vignette: 58-year-old woman with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes, sudden painless cloud of floaters, then haze, in the right eye this morning.

results.front_door: No chemical exposure, no injury, no lid cellulitis.
results.presentation: Right eye white and quiet; hand motion right, 20/40 left.
results.fundus_result: No afferent defect; no red reflex and no fundus view on the right; ultrasound shows mobile echoes in the vitreous with the retina flat. Left fundus: new vessels on the disc.

cases.label: Central retinal vein occlusion
cases.vignette: 70-year-old man with hypertension and glaucoma, woke with blurred vision in the right eye.

results.front_door: No chemical exposure, no injury, no lid cellulitis.
results.presentation: Right eye white and quiet; acuity 20/200 right, 20/25 left.
results.fundus_result: Mild right afferent defect; swollen disc, tortuous dilated veins and hemorrhages in all four quadrants.

cases.label: Swollen optic disc
cases.vignette: 71-year-old man, woke with the lower half of the vision in his right eye missing. No pain.

results.front_door: No chemical exposure, no injury, no lid cellulitis.
results.presentation: Right eye white and quiet; acuity 20/60 right, 20/20 left; lower field gone on the right.
results.fundus_result: Right afferent defect; swollen right disc with a few flame hemorrhages; no cherry-red spot; retina attached.
results.disc_esr: ESR 14, CRP normal; no headache, jaw pain or scalp tenderness.

cases.label: Hemianopia mistaken for one eye
cases.vignette: 72-year-old woman, since lunchtime she keeps bumping into things on her right and thinks her right eye has failed.

results.front_door: No chemical exposure, no injury, no lid cellulitis.
results.presentation: Both eyes white and quiet; acuity 20/25 each eye.
results.fundus_result: No afferent defect; normal fundus and ultrasound in both eyes. Fields: the right half is missing in both eyes.
